460.t: Favorite classical composers: Shostakovich, Strauss and the Russians
460.s: Laws talks about the composers he loves, citing Shostakovich's Eleventh Symphony premiere in Houston and Richard Strauss. He explains why Mozart does not move him.
460.q: Yeah. You know what? The composers that I’m really interested in and crazy about, it’s not so much that they write music for the flute. It’s just the overall musical content. For instance, one of my favorite pieces I heard premiered when I was going to that music appreciation – when I was required…

460.t: French composers and the pianist Eugene Maslov
460.s: Asked about Ravel and Debussy, Laws says the Russians appeal more. He praises the Russian pianist-composer Eugene Maslov, for whom top musicians played for free.
460.q: He played on it. And several other – I mean, top-notch musicians play for free. Why? Because this guy is such a high quality player and composer. You should hear it. Eugene Maslov. Stix heard it. That’s how I knew about him. Stix had me play on two of his records. But the guy can’t get arrested.…

460.t: Contemporary composers, Stravinsky and Boulez at the Philharmonic
460.s: Laws is not familiar with Messiaen or Ligeti, loves Stravinsky, and did not like Bartok. He recalls Pierre Boulez conducting modern music and Julius Baker's dislike of it.
460.q: No. I don’t know. I’m not too familiar with them, I should say. I’m not going to put down the compositions. I don’t – but Igor Stravinsky. Here again, he’s Russian. Stravinsky. I love his Firebird and his Rite of Spring.

460.t: Reaction to the Rite of Spring album
460.s: Brown says Laws's Rite of Spring album astonished him and James Newton. Laws says he did not understand the fuss and notes Sebesky's role.
460.ch: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
460.q: You know what? My brother – I really didn’t understand all the hullabaloo over that record. I really didn’t, because, to me, we just – in fact Don Sebesky was the one who . . .

321.t: Time machine to the Rite premiere; Ravel and Debussy
321.s: He would attend the 1913 premiere, and notes Ravel's influence and Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto.
321.q: Oh that one, for sure. And I even thought like you know when I had some grandiose ideas like there should be a movie of this opening night or whatever, and I think there is one

321.t: Stravinsky on expression, harmony, the octatonic scale and tempos
321.s: Danko discusses Stravinsky's Debussy and Ravel links, the diminished scale in jazz, the architecture of the piece and tempos for dancers.
321.q: Pretty wild. I remember reading that a long time ago. And, okay. It’s the way he — I mean I think it’s like, he’s like, at that point you know he’s friends with Ravel, he’s friends with Debussy. A lot of those kind of harmonies are present in Debussy a little less functional and Ravel almost…

321.t: Ebony Concerto, Woody Herman and imperfect spirit
321.s: They discuss the ragged Woody Herman Ebony Concerto and why energy matters more than perfection.
321.q: Hopefully that’s the spirit I’m bringing, you know, even when I do my gig tomorrow night. It ain’t going to be perfect. And one of the inspiring things, I talked about a few things in the liner notes that inspired me, but when I first heard, because I’d heard denigrating things about the Woody…

492.t: Stevens on Bartok, folk song and Fibonacci
492.s: Stevens tells Lloyd that Bartok's folk-song approach matches his own and that Bartok used Fibonacci numbers.
492.q: So he would have me up to his studio and stuff, and talk to me. He told me, he said, “What you like and what’s going on...” Aww man, it almost makes me cry, man. He said, “Bartok is dealing with his folk song, and that’s what you’re dealing with!”

492.t: Halsey Stevens and listening to Bartok in Memphis
492.s: Asked about Halsey Stevens, Lloyd says he and Booker listened to Bartok's Concerto for Orchestra and quartets back in Memphis.
492.q: Bartok. See, here’s the thing: Booker and I were listening to a lot of Bartok ­ Bartok’s Concerto for Orchestra...

492.t: Visiting Bartok's house and museum in Hungary
492.s: Lloyd and Dorothy are shown through the closed Bartok museum in Budapest and see film of Bartok playing.
492.q: One time Dorothy and I were in Hungary, and we took a car, and they took us out to Bartok’s house and stuff. It was closed up but they showed me where Bartok lived.

387.t: Meeting Stravinsky in Germany; his guiding composers
387.s: Stravinsky visited a rehearsal in Germany; Sauter names the composers who guide him.
387.q: had a job at a German radio station in '57 and he was over rehearsing to perform, Agon, and they brought him into our rehearsal. Unfortunately I'm the conductor.

387.s: Sauter's one meeting with Bartok and the lesson of spanning.
387.q: He was a diminutive little man, Szegedi's blazing eyes. They were at Sagetti's apartment, rehearsing "Contrasty" and during an intermission I was introduced to Bartok, as a young composer, which I was. I was young anyway.

387.t: Listening to classical records in the Norvo band
387.s: The band bought classical sets; jazz people loved Stravinsky and symphonic music, contrary to Hammond.
387.q: at this time and I began listening and of course so did Red and Mildred and so did the guys in the band. If they weren't going to clubs listening, we bought a record player. of our own and we listened to these things. It was sessions like that that I first came on (inaudible), and Le sacre du…

369.t: Favorite classical composers: Chopin, Mendelssohn, Beethoven, Grieg, Bach, Mozart
369.s: She comments on each composer's difficulty and character, from Chopin's delicacy to Bach's finger independence and Mozart's lightness.
369.q: I love him. He must be played delicately, softly and fast. He’s a very difficult composer.

369.t: Rachmaninoff's Third Concerto when she is down
369.s: She works on the Rachmaninoff Third for its many notes and hears spirituals and jazz themes in his music.
369.q: Especially the Rachmaninoff Third. In some of his music you can hear themes that could be presented as jazz.

225.t: Stravinsky, Ravel, Bartok and Bloch listening; Israel
225.s: His collection of recordings, Schelomo, and Carisi's Israel from Birth of the Cool.
225.q: And will always be. I began to listen to Stravinsky’s other works. Then I became aware of Ravel and Bartok and became a real addict of these persons in particular: Stravinsky, Ravel, Bartok, Prokofiev, Richard Strauss, people of that era. I must have five different recordings of Le Sacre [Le Sacre…

225.t: Coloristic writing and discovering classical music through Johnny Carisi
225.s: Hearing The Rite of Spring at Carisi's home turned Johnson into a classical music devotee.
225.q: Dave, I had by that time really started to pay attention to classical music, per se. I loved classical music. That started during the so-called Thirdstream cycle in the evolution of jazz where I became very friendly and closely associated with the activities of Gunther Schuller on the one hand,…

508.t: Favorite classical composers and melody in the avant-garde
508.s: He lists Bach, Prokofiev, Barber, Wagner and others, and likes any music with melody, even Berg and Hindemith.
508.q: There’s a lot of them. Bach and … he’s the king. And Mozart, Shostakovich, Prokofiev is really undervalued, but he is quite amazing. Stravinsky’s great. Samuel Barber is fantastic as an American composer. Aaron Copland is great. Benjamin Britten is great. Wagner, love the man. Love …especially the…

508.t: Prokofiev's career, Cold War perception and Ornette as inside music
508.s: Prokofiev was overlooked next to Stravinsky and Rachmaninoff; he compares this to how Ornette's music was perceived as out when it was inside.
508.q: Yeah. Prokofiev, I like him better that Bartok, actually. Prokofiev is …his string quartets …you could put them up there next to Shostakovich, although nobody talks about them. And his operas are incredible. And his ballets are incredible. He didn’t really write a lot of symphonies. Neither did…

148.t: Other Gershwin, and Bernstein's West Side Story
148.s: He enjoys Gershwin's piano works and praises West Side Story for breaking song forms.
148.q: I think that his West Side Story was very innovative in terms of songs, in terms of the form of American songs, pop tunes, things that became popular. He didn't hold to the thirty two bars, he didn't hold to the acceptable harmonies.

148.s: He admires Porgy and Bess, thanks Schillinger for enabling it, and declines to guess Gershwin's later direction.
148.q: As I was saying, methods-- I can't get along with methods--not that I can't get along, I can't use them to write with. I can't get a method to come out of me. Nevertheless, I thank God that there was a guy like Schillinger who came along and invented this method so that a guy like Gershwin could…

448.t: Bechet's classical record and Will Marion Cook
448.s: The Paris ballet record and Bechet's idealisation of soloing before an orchestra, rooted in his early Will Marion Cook experience.
448.q: Yeah, the classical record made in Paris. In Paris, yeah. Yeah, I did. In fact, I heard it before it came out because Sidney came over here in the early 50s with the test pressings on it.

279.s: Short exchange on Bix's liking for classical music and Hug's conversation with him.
279.ch: Whiteman at the St. Charles Theater
279.q: Yeah, I don't know. Yeah, it really stopped you. Yeah. When you stop to think of it. That's right.

47.t: Bix and the Wolverines loving symphonic music
47.s: The group went to hear the Cincinnati Symphony and New York Philharmonic; Bix's love of Debussy, Eastwood Lane and MacDowell.
47.q: We all did. We all loved it. And the proof of the pudding is that the first night we were together in five years in New York City, we don't go to hear a jam band. We go to hear the New York Philharmonic Symphony. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

652.t: Bernard Heiden and the Bartok sonata
652.s: Studying Bartok in Heiden's arranging class, the music looked fantastic but sounded like garbage men.
652.q: Yeah. You just reminded me of something. I took arranging in college from Bernard Heiden. Do you recall him? Composer? He was at IU. Anyhow we had several classes, two semesters of it, and he got to talking and analyzing the Bartok Fourth Violin Sonata I guess it was. Okay. So as soon as class was…

787.t: A favorite dissonance in Stravinsky's 'Agon' and 'The Rite of Spring'
787.s: He names the opening of Stravinsky's 'Agon' as his favorite dissonance, and says Mahler helped him understand the orchestration of 'The Rite of Spring'.
787.q: Actually I do. How about that? Who would have thought that question, Monk? Here it is [plays]. It’s this [plays]. It’s the opening of Stravinsky’s wonderful ballet “Agon.” If you don’t know it it’s a magnificently compact orchestral piece of — what do you say — of episodes you know, for two…

746.s: She loves African and Scandinavian folk music and mentions Hardanger fiddle player Benedicte Maurseth.
746.q: Yeah, yeah. Very much, very, very much, folk music from everywhere, especially Africa, all the different African countries. Amazing music. Amazing folk music from all over the world really. I also love Scandinavian folk music very much and I remember when I first listened to a recording I was…

993.t: Stravinsky, new music and African influence on composition
993.s: Rowe links the trio to The Rite of Spring; Daley compares Stravinsky's structure and sources to improvisation, and values screams and colors.
993.q: Exactly. See that’s the thing. I mean that’s the thing about the whole new music, what they call the new music classical scene, you know. What happens is that for some strange reason, you know, like people like to divide people and put them in boxes and everything. No. If you go to a new music…

539.t: Preferring first albums and one-of-a-kind artists
539.s: Dorn says he likes first albums and original artists with world-class chops.
539.q: Well I like first albums. I like world class artists who are original. So I’ve always been drawn to anything from Rufus Harley to Bette Midler to Leon Redbone to Rahsaan. That’s what I like — one of a kind artists with world class chops. And I like them in the

835.t: Dave Brubeck, Greek rhythms and preparing for Ellis's music
835.s: Rowe cites Brubeck and Greek music; Humphrey says playing along with Brubeck records prepared him for Don Ellis's music.
835.q: Yeah they did. I mean I guess I must have subjectively understood what it was. I didn’t objectively be able to explain except I just heard it and I played along with those records and tried to learn as much about it as possible. And I think that was probably the main reason why I was able to…

546.s: Shostakovich is his favourite composer for his motivic development; he compares him to Beethoven and discusses Beethoven's debt to Haydn.
546.q: Dmitri Shostakovich. Since I was a kid, his music has spoken to me, and now as a quote unquote scholar or whatever I am, then I really appreciate his sense of motific development. He is the twentieth century Beethoven. You know [scats] think about how far that went with those four notes, three of…

994.t: Listener reactions, Baroque connections and influences
994.s: Listeners interpret instrumental music freely; Rowe hears Baroque architecture; Scales names Bach, Mozart, Stravinsky, Fleck, Corea, Metheny and hip-hop artists as influences.
994.q: Yeah. I think that sometimes people will say things – I wish I could think of something right now that would be so cool, but yeah with instrumental music it’s all open to interpretation. So you know I do have to go back, “Can you tell me certain things is,” where my music has struck them in a…

932.s: Shear names Max Steiner, Bernard Herrmann, Jerry Goldsmith and Korngold as favorites.
932.q: Oh gosh, well Max Steiner from the early days of film was one of the greats. I think Bernard Herrmann, who did Psycho, the movie Psycho. And he really changed the way, especially strings are scored in films. And Bernard Herrmann, he did a lot of the “Twilight Zones” early on. And then he did many…

141.t: Twentieth-century classical listening at LSU and the Bartok link
141.s: At LSU he began listening to modern classical music; Bartok's Hungarian Sketches fed the Back Country Suite.

61.t: Contemporary classical music and Stravinsky in Boston
61.s: From Debussy and Varese to Stravinsky at Harvard-era Boston, prepared him for Cage and Hovhaness.
61.q: Oh, no problem. I’d already started getting interested in – of course, I’d studied piano, but I never got better than playing a version of Für Elise by Beethoven which was unique in the annals of classical music. I never heard another pianist play it the way I played it. I don’t think any other…

133.t: Classical taste: Stravinsky, Gershwin, Mozart and Bartok
133.s: He recounts hearing The Rite of Spring in college and says he prefers modern composers like Stravinsky and Shostakovich over Mozart, with a liking for Bartok.
133.ch: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
133.q: Yeah, I just don't, uh, there's two sides to that. I, when I'm exposed to it, you know, I'm like a, you know, somebody with their mouth open, especially when it's at this level, you know. Stravinsky's uh, uh, not the uh, Rites of Spring. I'll always remember when I first heard that. It may be the…

165.s: He prefers the term symphonic to classical, loves Tchaikovsky and Chopin, and notes composers borrowing Chopin.
165.q: I agree with what Duke Ellington said: “There are only two kinds of music. Good music” and all that other kind. So I listen to everything. I have many symphonic pieces. I use the term “symphonic,” because I think the term “classical” is elitist and suggestive that other types of music cannot also…

111.t: Elvin's own listening: Bobby Timmons, pygmy recordings, classical
111.s: He tells of Bobby Timmons's pygmy record and says he loves Stravinsky and Casals.
111.q: Yeah, Timmons. Well he lives right there on East 6th street, and he lived right across the street from me. So he came over to my house once and he had this record and he said, “What are they doing?” You know it was a song, and he said, “When did they come to the end of it? What’s the phrasing?” I…

493.t: Composing influences and falling for classical music
493.s: His composing drew on anything that sounded good. He tells how Holst's The Planets and Stravinsky, especially The Rite of Spring, grabbed him in 1992.
493.q: Wow. The reason why I have to say wow is because really the influences was anything that sounded good to me. I did have jazz influences, but it was also influences from classical music, like, for example – and I want to go back to classical music just for a little bit, because it was around this…

228.t: Stravinsky, Bartok and widening his writing
228.s: The day Bird died McLean bought Rite of Spring, which opened new directions, as it had for Tristano.
228.ch: Blue Note, The Connection and Tony Williams
228.q: I think it was because I had listened to some other music that I hadn’t experienced before. Like Bird told me early on to listen to Stravinsky, Rites of Spring, and I didn’t pay that any attention at all. In fact, I thought he was trying to throw me off, send me off to listen to some of this…

104.t: Never meeting Leonard Bernstein, and West Side Story tunes
104.s: She never met Bernstein, loved West Side Story and tried unsuccessfully to get him on Piano Jazz.
104.q: I never did meet him. I loved all that music. I went to see the West Side Story. I play a lot of his music, or more then than I do now. Somehow for a time everybody was playing everything from the West Side Story. Then it went out of fashion. But the tunes are just as great as they ever were. Bill…

408.s: Bach and Bird, Beethoven and Brahms, and Latin and flamenco music.
408.q: to be able to read a little bit, you know. Learn some keyboard, learn some keyboard harmony. Be able to write a little tune, understand fugal techniques, understand the Bach, Beethoven, Brahms. I mean, if you’re going to play bebop, um I mean, I think Bach is to fugal technique what Bird is to…

26.t: Classical musicians who came to hear the band; the Capitol Theatre pit band
26.s: Classical musicians admired the band; Greer and Duke studied the Capitol Theatre orchestra.
26.ch: Leaving the band, Strayhorn and reflections
26.q: All of them. All of them. You see, those long-haired musicians, you know, they loved what they heard. But they never played with us, so they used to come just to enjoy the music, being classical musicians. They'd come and enjoy the band, you know, all them guys. They were friends of Duke, they…

117.t: Classical music Bix introduced to the Chicagoans
117.s: Freeman recalls listening to Stravinsky, Ravel, Debussy and others through Bix, a fine pianist.
117.ch: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
117.q: Oh, yes, you know, in those days, we listened to music that had nothing to do with jazz as many of the great players had, black or white. We listened to people like Stravinsky, Jacque Ibert, Ravel, Debussy,

454.t: Beethoven: discovering he was black, and the string quartets
454.s: Mingus came to Beethoven late, after learning he was black, and loves the late quartets.
454.q: Funky. People don't think of John Lewis as being funky, but he's very funky. Funny (inaudible) Well, we're still on the question of who influenced me, who my favorite musicians were. I didn't get into Beethoven until much later, see, when I found out he was black. See, I didn't know he was black, a…

169.s: Charlie Parker played Stravinsky's Rite of Spring for McGhee, who then bought more.
169.ch: Georgie Auld, Hawkins and Los Angeles
169.q: those guys. I didn't know nothin' about Stravinsky. So Bird was the first one to tell me about it. So like, The Rite of Spring, he brought it over to the house and let me hear it. And I said, "Yeah, this cat, he's kind of cool, you know; he knows what he's doing." Then I went and got a couple of…

389.t: Bix's classical listening at the hotel suite
389.s: Bix visited Challis's hotel suite to listen to Debussy and other impressionist works.
389.q: Oh, yeah, fine appreciation for music. Fine. Of course, I have sat with him at nights, nothing else would do, we would go over -- I had a suite in the hotel there and he had a little joint over in a place called the Billinghurst. They used to call them flea bags, and a lot of the musicians stayed…
